parsing_res_list.block_content: The closed ties must conform to the following:
1.The ties shall be at least #3 bars for longitudinal bars #8 or smaller and at least #4 bars for #9 longitudinal bars or greater.
2.To ensure full development, the ties shall be closed using 135-degree hooks. The use of 90-degree bends is not recommended.
3.The vertical spacing of the ties shall not exceed 16 longitudinal bar diameters, 48 tie diameters, or ½ of the least dimension of the column section.

4.The ties shall be located vertically not more than ½ the tie spacing above the top of footing or slab and not more than ½ the tie spacing below the lowest horizontal reinforcement in a slab or drop panel. Where beams frame into a column, the ties may be terminated not more than 3 inches below the lowest reinforcement in the shallowest of the beams.

5.The ties shall be arranged such that every corner and alternate longitudinal bar shall have lateral support provided by the corner of a tie with an included angle of not more than 135 degrees and no bar shall be farther than 6 inches clear on each side along the tie from such a laterally supported bar.

The above requirements for the lateral ties ensure that buckling of the longitudinal reinforcement in compression will not occur. However, if the section is subjected to large shear or torsional stresses, the closed ties must be increased in accordance with the provisions established for beams (see Section 4-39).

Spiral columns may be subjected to significant bending moments about both axes and should, therefore, be designed for biaxial bending. However, due to the uniform distribution of the longitudinal reinforcement in the form of a circle, the bending moment (or eccentricities) in each direction can be resolved into a resultant bending moment (or eccentricity). The closed ties must conform to the following:
The ties shall be at least #3 bars for longitudinal bars #8 or smaller and at
least #4 bars for #9 longitudinal bars or greater.
To ensure full development, the ties shall be closed using 135-degree
hooks. The use of 90-degree bends is not recommended.
The vertical spacing of the ties shall not exceed 16 longitudinal bar
diameters, 48 tie diameters, or ½ of the least dimension of the column
section.
The ties shall be located vertically not more than ½ the tie spacing above
the top of footing or slab and not more than ½ the tie spacing below the
lowest horizontal reinforcement in a slab or drop panel. Where beams
frame into a column, the ties may be terminated not more than 3 inches
below the lowest reinforcement in the shallowest of the beams.
The ties shall be arranged such that every corner and alternate
longitudinal bar shall have lateral support provided by the corner of a tie
with an included angle of not more than 135 degrees and no bar shall be
farther than 6 inches clear on each side along the tie from such a laterally
supported bar.
The above requirements for the lateral ties ensure that buckling of the longitudinal
reinforcement in compression will not occur. However, if the section is subjected to
large shear or torsional stresses, the closed ties must be increased in accordance with
the provisions established for beams (see Section 4-39).
DESIGN OF SPIRAL COLUMNS.
General.
Spiral columns may be subjected to significant bending moments about both axes and
should, therefore, be designed for biaxial bending. However, due to the uniform
distribution of the longitudinal reinforcement in the form of a circle, the bending moment
(or eccentricities) in each direction can be resolved into a resultant bending moment (or
eccentricity). The column can then be designed for uniaxial bending using Equations
4-161 and 4-166 for the regions where compression and tension control the design,
respectively.
Minimum Eccentricity.
